newsitem.title: USA: Fortune 500 profits up 23.3 pct; GM tops list.
newsitem.headline: Fortune 500 profits up 23.3 pct; GM tops list.

text.p: Profits for the Fortune 500 firms rose a record 23.3 percent in 1996, on combined revenue growth of 8.3 percent, as the largest companies in America continue to squeeze more profit from each dollar of sales, Fortune magazine reported in its April 28 edition.
General Motors Corp. retained its No. 1 spot among the list of Fortune 500 firms, even with a 0.3 percent drop in revenues to $168.5 billion.
Retaining the No. 2 spot was Ford Motor Co., with a 7.2 percent revenue gain to $146.99 billion. Also, keeping steady at No. 3 was Exxon, with an 8.6 percent revenue gain over 1995 to $119.4 billion.
The Fortune 500 is Fortune Magazine's annual ranking of the nation's largest corporations. Fortune, published by Time Warner Inc. unit Time Inc., has been compiling the list for 42 years.
Fortune said that of the 305 companies on the Fortune 500 list that reported profit increases last year, 78 percent of them had earnings grow faster than revenues.

"I don't see that as a positive sign," said Stephen Roach, chief economist at Morgan Stanley. "Corporate America has gotten very good at focusing on operational effectiveness, but in doing that, it has dropped the ball on sustainable growth."
In 1996, profits for the Fortune 500 grew 23.3 percent to $301 billion, while revenues grew 8.3 percent to $5.077 trillion.
A year earlier, profits grew 13.4 percent to $244 billion, on revenue growth of 9.9 percent to $4.690 trillion.

The magazine said General Electric Co. and AT&T Corp. switched positions on the 500's Top 10 list. GE, which was No. 7 in 1995, moved up to No. 5. AT&T moved down to No. 7 from the No. 5 spot in 1995.

Other companies rounding out the Top Ten are: Ford, No. 2; Exxon, No. 3; Wal-Mart Stores Corp., No. 4; International Business Machines Corp., No. 6; Mobil Corp., No. 8; Chrysler Corp., No. 9; and Philip Morris Cos. Inc, No. 10.
In terms of number of employees, Wal-Mart Stores topped the list with 675,000 employees. General Motors came in second with 647,000; Pepsico third with 486,000 and Ford fourth with 371,702.
Merger mania led to huge revenue increases, with the list for revenue gainers led by Medpartners, which acquired Caremark International, with a 563.3 percent gain to $4.813 billion.
Exxon had the highest profits, with a 16.1 percent gain over 1995 to $7.51 billion.
A big looser on the Fortune 500 list was General Mills Inc., which dropped in rank to 264 from 156. To blame: cereal price cuts, which caused revenues to fall.
